\chapter{Whose, and Who To}
\label{ch:ur-whose-and-who-to}
\hlchaptermodality{26}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say whose something is for any person, mark when the owner is also the subject, invite agreement, and call somebody.}

The possessive column fills from two of six to five of six, and \ur{اپنا} adds a distinction English has not got at all -- his own room against somebody else's -- which Urdu requires and a learner cannot skip.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[is kā]{\ur{اس} \ur{کا} (is kā) — his, her}

\label{lesson:UR-C26-is-ka}



\begin{quote}
What is the oblique of \textbf{\ur{یہ}}? Then say \textbf{our room}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the shape a noun takes before a postposition — \emph{kamre}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{اس} \ur{کا}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{اس} \ur{کا} \ur{کمرہ}} — \emph{is kā kamrā} — \textbf{his room}, or \textbf{her room.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ان} \ur{کا} \ur{کمرہ}} — \emph{un kā kamrā} — \textbf{their room}, or \textbf{his room}, respectfully.
\end{quote}

Urdu has no word for \emph{his} and none for \emph{her}. It takes the demonstrative in the oblique shape you learned two chapters ago and puts \textbf{\ur{کا}} after it — which is why this could not be taught earlier. The third-person possessive is built on the oblique, and until the oblique existed there was nothing to build it on.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the column, finally full}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{possessive} & \textbf{written} \\
\midrule
I & \textbf{\ur{میرا}} & fused \\
we & \textbf{\ur{ہمارا}} & fused \\
you, respectfully & \textbf{\ur{آپ} \ur{کا}} & apart \\
he, she, it & \textbf{\ur{اس} \ur{کا}} & apart \\
they, or he respectfully & \textbf{\ur{ان} \ur{کا}} & apart \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Five of the six an A1 candidate needs, and the shape of the sixth — \emph{your}, to somebody close — follows the same rule.

Every one of them ends in \textbf{-\ur{ا}} and agrees like an adjective, so \textbf{\ur{اس} \ur{کی} \ur{ماں}} is \emph{his mother} and \textbf{\ur{اس} \ur{کے} \ur{کمرے} \ur{میں}} is \emph{in his room}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{is kā kamrā}
  \item the respectful one — \emph{un kā kamrā}
  \item the whole column — \emph{merā}, \emph{hamārā}, \emph{āp kā}, \emph{is kā}, \emph{un kā}
  \item agreeing — \emph{is kī māṅ}, \emph{is ke kamre meṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does Urdu have a word for \textbf{his}? (\textbf{No} — it uses \textbf{\ur{اس}} plus \textbf{\ur{کا}}.) Why could this not be taught before chapter twenty-four? (\textbf{It needs the oblique demonstrative}.) And what does the \textbf{\ur{کا}} agree with? (\textbf{The noun after it}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[apnā]{\ur{اپنا} (apnā) — one's own}

\label{lesson:UR-C26-apna}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{his room}, then \textbf{our room}. Then say \textbf{my name}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{اپنا}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میں} \ur{اپنے} \ur{کمرے} \ur{میں} \ur{ہوں}} — \emph{maiṅ apne kamre meṅ hūṅ} — \textbf{I am in my (own) room.}
\end{quote}

Here is a rule English does not have and Urdu will not let you skip. When the owner is \textbf{the same person as the subject of the sentence}, Urdu replaces the ordinary possessive with \textbf{\ur{اپنا}}.

So it is \textbf{\ur{میرا} \ur{کمرہ}} when somebody else is speaking about my room, and \textbf{\ur{اپنا} \ur{کمرہ}} the moment \emph{I} am the one doing something in it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: getting it wrong changes the meaning}]
This is not a politeness or a nicety. The two sentences mean different things:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Urdu} & \textbf{what it means} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ur{وہ} \ur{اپنے} \ur{کمرے} \ur{میں} \ur{ہے}} & he is in \textbf{his own} room \\
\textbf{\ur{وہ} \ur{اس} \ur{کے} \ur{کمرے} \ur{میں} \ur{ہے}} & he is in \textbf{somebody else's} room \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An English speaker hears \emph{he is in his room} for both and has no way to tell them apart. Urdu marks the difference and requires you to.

\textbf{\ur{اپنا}} agrees like every other possessive: \textbf{\ur{اپنا} \ur{کمرہ}}, \textbf{\ur{اپنی} \ur{ماں}}, \textbf{\ur{اپنے} \ur{کمرے} \ur{میں}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maiṅ apne kamre meṅ hūṅ}
  \item the pair that differ — \emph{voh apne kamre meṅ hai}, \emph{voh is ke kamre meṅ hai}
  \item agreeing — \emph{apnā kamrā}, \emph{apnī māṅ}
  \item with we — \emph{ham apne kamre meṅ haiṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
When must you use \textbf{\ur{اپنا}}? (\textbf{When the owner is the subject of the sentence}.) What does \textbf{\ur{وہ} \ur{اس} \ur{کے} \ur{کمرے} \ur{میں} \ur{ہے}} mean? (\textbf{He is in somebody else's room}.) And does \textbf{\ur{اپنا}} agree? (\textbf{Yes} — like every possessive.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hai nā?]{\ur{ہے} \ur{نا؟} (hai nā?) — isn't it?}

\label{lesson:UR-C26-hai-na}



\begin{quote}
Ask a yes-or-no question with \textbf{\ur{کیا}}. Then say the negator that stands in front of a refused noun.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{ہے} \ur{نا؟}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{آپ} \ur{یہاں} \ur{ہیں،} \ur{ہے} \ur{نا؟}} — \emph{āp yahāṅ haiṅ, hai nā?} — \textbf{you are here, aren't you?}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{یہ} \ur{آپ} \ur{کا} \ur{کمرہ} \ur{ہے،} \ur{ہے} \ur{نا؟}} — \textbf{this is your room, isn't it?}
\end{quote}

Both halves have been in this book for twenty-five chapters. \textbf{\ur{ہے}} arrived in chapter two and \textbf{\ur{نہ}} in chapter nineteen, and nobody has ever put them together. It is not a new word; it is an assembly.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two ways to ask, and they mean different things}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{how you ask} & \textbf{what it says} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ur{کیا}} … \emph{āp ṭhīk haiṅ?} & I do not know. Tell me. \\
\emph{āp ṭhīk haiṅ}, \textbf{\ur{ہے} \ur{نا؟}} & I think so. Agree with me. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Chapter nineteen's \textbf{\ur{کیا}} opens a genuine question. The tag makes a statement and asks the listener to confirm it, and a conversation runs on the second far more than on the first.

The reply is the \emph{jī hāṅ} of chapter one. (\emph{Ṭhīk} and \emph{jī} stay in romanization: between them they need three letters the script ladder has not reached.)
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āp yahāṅ haiṅ, hai nā?}
  \item the two ways, back to back — \emph{kyā āp ṭhīk haiṅ?}, then \emph{āp ṭhīk haiṅ, hai nā?}
  \item and the reply — \emph{jī hāṅ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the difference between asking with \textbf{\ur{کیا}} and asking with the tag? (\textbf{\ur{کیا}} asks; the tag \textbf{invites agreement}.) Which two pieces make the tag, and how old are they? (\textbf{\ur{ہے}} from chapter two and \textbf{\ur{نہ}} from chapter nineteen.) And what do you reply? (\emph{Jī hāṅ}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[māṅ!]{\ur{ماں}! (māṅ!) — calling somebody}

\label{lesson:UR-C26-vocative}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{mother}. Then say the greeting from chapter one, and ask yourself who you said it \emph{to}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the kin term as an address}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ماں}! \ur{سلام}} — \emph{māṅ! salām} — \textbf{Mother! Hello.}
\end{quote}

This book has taught \textbf{\ur{ماں}} since chapter seventeen as a noun — a person you can \emph{talk about}. Not once has anybody been \textbf{called}.

That matters more in Urdu than in English. An Urdu speaker addresses almost nobody by name. A mother is \textbf{\ur{ماں}}, an older brother is \emph{bhāī}, a shopkeeper is \emph{bhāī}, a stranger of your parents' age is \emph{uncle} or \emph{auntie}. Using a first name where a kin term is expected is the mistake, not the other way round.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what the vocative does to the noun}]
Urdu kept a fragment of the old vocative case, and it is one letter's worth:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the noun} & \textbf{talking about} & \textbf{calling} \\
\midrule
ends in \emph{-ā} & \textbf{\ur{کمرہ}} & \textbf{\ur{کمرے}} \\
plural & \textbf{\ur{کمروں}} (before a postposition) & \textbf{\ur{کمرو}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The call form of a plural is \textbf{-\ur{و}}, not the \textbf{-\ur{وں}} you learned in chapter twenty-five. The nasal drops. That is the whole difference between shouting to a group and saying something about them.

\textbf{\ur{ماں}} does not end in \textbf{-\ur{ا}}, so it does not change — which is why calling your mother is the easiest vocative in the language.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{māṅ! salām}
  \item the two plural endings — \emph{kamroṅ meṅ} (about), \emph{kamro} (calling)
  \item greeting and then checking — \emph{māṅ! āp yahāṅ haiṅ, hai nā?}
  \item the habit — a name is the exception, a kin term is the rule
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does an Urdu speaker usually address somebody? (\textbf{By a kin term}, not a name.) What is the plural call form? (\textbf{-\ur{و}}, with the nasal dropped.) And why does \textbf{\ur{ماں}} not change? (\textbf{It does not end in \emph{-ā}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[is kā · apnā · hai nā? · māṅ!]{Whose, and who to}

\label{lesson:UR-R26-whose-and-who-to}



\begin{quote}
Say the whole possessive column. Then say which of its members you must swap out when the owner is also the subject, and what you swap it for.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{merā}, \emph{hamārā}, \emph{āp kā}, \emph{is kā}, \emph{un kā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the pair that differ — \emph{voh apne kamre meṅ hai}, \emph{voh is ke kamre meṅ hai}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the tag — \emph{āp yahāṅ haiṅ, hai nā?}
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the oblique of \emph{yih} — \emph{is}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — four chapters of shapes, run cold}
Four chapters ago no Urdu noun in this book changed shape, nothing was anywhere, nobody was more than one, and nobody but you and the person in front of you could own anything. Run the whole distance, cold.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four shapes — \emph{kamrā}, \emph{kamre}, \emph{kamre meṅ}, \emph{kamroṅ meṅ}
  \item and the fifth, for calling — \emph{kamro}
  \item the demonstratives bending — \emph{is kamre meṅ}, \emph{un kamroṅ meṅ}
  \item the possessives agreeing — \emph{is kā kamrā}, \emph{is kī māṅ}, \emph{is ke kamre meṅ}
  \item one's own — \emph{maiṅ apne kamre meṅ hūṅ}, \emph{ham apne kamre meṅ haiṅ}
  \item placed, with a colour — \emph{nīle kamre meṅ}
  \item the pantry and the weather — \emph{chāy yahāṅ hai}, \emph{garmī hai, hai nā?}
  \item calling, then greeting, then checking — \emph{māṅ! salām. āp yahāṅ haiṅ, hai nā?}
  \item to whom — \emph{is ko}, \emph{un ko}, \emph{māṅ ko}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does Urdu have a word for \emph{his}? (\textbf{No} — the oblique plus \textbf{\ur{کا}}.) When is \textbf{\ur{اپنا}} compulsory? (\textbf{When the owner is the subject}.) What does the tag do that \textbf{\ur{کیا}} does not? (\textbf{Invite agreement}.) And how do you call somebody? (\textbf{By a kin term}, with the plural ending \textbf{-\ur{و}}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
